title: Homing and limits
goals: Say which axes need homing after power-up, and which do not
Put the steps of a switch-and-index homing sequence in order, and say why it ends slowly
Choose between switch homing, index homing and hard-stop homing
Set software limits, hard limits and end stops in the right order along the travel
Say why limit switches are wired normally closed
summary:
An axis with an **incremental** encoder only counts movement from wherever it was when it powered up, so it must **home**: find a known place and call it zero (or a set value). An **absolute** encoder knows its angle at power-up; a **multi-turn** absolute knows its whole position, so needs no homing in daily use (its zero is set once, at commissioning).

A good **homing sequence**:

1. Move towards the **home switch** at a fair speed
2. Find the switch, stop, **back off** until it clears
3. Approach again **slowly**, always from the **same direction**, and latch the switch's edge
4. Optionally carry on to the encoder's next **index pulse** (Z, once a turn) for a repeatable zero
5. Apply the **home offset** and set the position

The index pulse is repeatable to a count; a switch edge only to the switch's own repeatability, worse at speed. Approaching from one direction takes out backlash.

**Hard-stop homing**: drive gently, at a low torque limit, against a mechanical stop, detect the stall, and back off. No switch, but it must be gentle.

**Limits**, from the middle of the travel outwards:

- **software limits** (the controller refuses to move beyond them; only valid once homed)
- **hard limit switches** (overtravel): just beyond, stop the axis in that direction
- **mechanical end stops** or buffers: the last resort

Limit switches are wired **normally closed**, so a broken wire or a missing switch looks like a limit and stops the axis: fail-safe.

These limits protect the machine. They are not safety functions for people unless designed as such (EN ISO 13849, a drive's safe limited position).

bench.task: On a servo or stepper axis at work, with the machine in a safe state for jogging and you authorised to run it, watch it home and check its limits.
check: Watch the homing: fast search, back-off, slow approach? Which direction does it finish in?
Note the home offset and the software limits in the controller
Find the hard limit switches: are they wired normally closed?
Check where the mechanical stops are, beyond the hard limits

cards.q: A servo axis with an incremental encoder loses power mid-move and is switched back on. What does the controller know about the axis's position?
options: Nothing reliable until it homes again
Exactly where it stopped, from the encoder
Its position to within one turn
Where it was before the move began
cards.why: An incremental encoder only sends pulses as it moves; the count lives in the controller. After a power cut (or any movement while off) the count is lost. It must home, or have an absolute encoder.

cards.title: Which axes need homing
cards.body:
- **Incremental encoder** (or a stepper counting steps): counts movement from power-up. Must **home** every time it powers up.
- **Single-turn absolute**: knows its angle within one turn, not how many turns. Still needs homing on a multi-turn axis.
- **Multi-turn absolute**: knows its whole position at power-up (by gears inside, or a battery). No homing in daily use: its zero is set once, at commissioning.

After a crash, a slipped coupling or a motor change, even an absolute axis needs its zero checked.
cards.more:
An incremental encoder is a tally counter: click, click, click. Switch it off and the count is gone, and if someone turns the shaft while it is off, nothing is counted.

An absolute encoder is a ruler: it reads its position directly, whenever asked.

The zero of an absolute encoder is stored as an offset in the drive or controller. If the coupling between motor and screw slips, or the motor is replaced, the encoder still reads an angle, but it no longer means the same place on the machine: set the offset again.

cards.q: Match each feedback with what it knows at power-up.
pairs: Nothing: it counts steps from power-up

cards.title: A good homing sequence
cards.body:
1. Move towards the **home switch** at a fair speed.
2. When the switch makes, stop and **back off** until it clears.
3. Come back **slowly**, from the **same direction** every time, and latch the position as the switch makes.
4. Optionally continue to the encoder's next **index pulse** (Z), and latch that.
5. Add the **home offset** and set the axis position.

Fast to find it, slow to measure it.
cards.more:
Why not just latch at speed? The switch and the input take a little time to react. At 200 mm/s, 1 ms of delay is 0.2 mm, and it varies. At 5 mm/s it is 0.005 mm.

Why back off? So the slow approach starts from a known side, and so the switch's own hysteresis (it makes at one place and breaks at another) is always crossed the same way.

Why the same direction? A screw or gearbox has backlash: approaching from the left and from the right gives two different positions for the same reading. Always finishing in one direction takes it out.

On a Galil controller, for example: FE finds a switch's edge, FI finds an index pulse, and HM does both in turn.

cards.q: Why does a homing sequence make its final approach to the switch slowly?
options: So the switch's delay moves the latched position very little
So the motor stays cool during homing
So the encoder can count every single pulse
Because the switch is damaged by fast approaches
cards.why: Any delay between the switch making and the position being latched becomes distance: speed × delay. At a slow creep that distance is tiny and repeatable.

cards.title: Switch or index pulse
cards.body:
A **home switch** (proximity sensor or mechanical switch) gets you near: repeatable to its own spec, maybe a few hundredths of a millimetre at a creep, worse at speed or as it warms.

The encoder's **index pulse** (Z channel) comes once per encoder turn, at the same angle every time: repeatable to about **one count**.

So precise axes home **to the switch, then to the next index pulse**. The switch says which turn; the index pulse says exactly where in it. Make sure the switch edge sits well **between** two index pulses, or a small change can make it pick the next one: a whole turn out.
cards.more:
Like finding a house: the switch tells you the street, the index tells you the door.

The catch: if the switch happens to make right next to where an index pulse falls, then on one day it makes just before, and the next pulse is the near one; another day just after, and the axis homes to the following pulse, one full turn later. On a 10 mm lead screw that is a 10 mm error that comes and goes.

The fix is to adjust the switch (or the home offset) so its edge sits about half a turn from an index pulse. Many controllers report the distance between the switch and the index after homing for exactly this check.

cards.q: An axis homes to its switch, then to the next index pulse. Every so often it homes exactly one screw lead out. What is the likely cause?
options: The switch edge sits right next to an index pulse
The encoder is losing counts at speed
The screw has worn at the home end
The software limits are set too close
cards.why: If the switch makes almost exactly where an index pulse falls, small variations decide whether the next pulse is this one or the one a turn later. Move the switch (or the offset) so its edge is about half a turn from the index.

cards.title: Homing without a switch: hard stop
cards.body:
Some axes home against a **mechanical stop**: the drive runs slowly with a **low torque (current) limit** until the axis stalls against the stop, detects it (current at the limit, or a rising following error), then backs off by a set distance and calls that home.

No switch or wiring, and very repeatable on a stiff stop. But it must be **gentle**: a full-torque crash into the stop damages the mechanics, so the torque limit and speed must be low and only raised again after homing.
cards.more:
It is like finding the end of a dark corridor by walking slowly with a hand out.

Used on grippers, small slides and actuators, where a switch would be awkward. The stop must be solid and must not move: if a bolt loosens, home moves with it.

A following error is the gap between where the controller wants the axis and where it is. Pushing against a stop, the command keeps going while the axis stays still, so the error grows: that is how the controller knows it has arrived.

cards.q: What is essential when an axis homes against a hard stop?
options: A low torque limit and a slow speed
A normally open home switch
An absolute multi-turn encoder
Full torque, so it seats firmly
cards.why: The axis drives into the stop on purpose, so it must do it gently: a low current limit and a slow speed. Full torque would damage the mechanics and could move the stop.

cards.title: Three layers of limits
cards.body:
From the middle of the travel outwards:

1. **Software limits**: the controller refuses to move beyond them. They only mean anything once the axis is **homed**.
2. **Hard limit switches** (overtravel): just beyond the software limits. If the axis reaches one, it **stops** and will only move back the other way.
3. **Mechanical end stops** (buffers): the last resort, beyond the switches.

So a fault has to get past each in turn before it reaches the next.
cards.more:
Like the barriers on a car park ramp: a painted line, then a kerb, then a wall.

The software limit stops a normal program from asking for an impossible move. If something goes wrong (lost position, a bad homing, a runaway), the hard limit switch stops it. If even that fails, the buffer takes the hit.

Set the software limits a little inside the switches, and the switches a little inside the stops, with enough room between each for the axis to stop from full speed. To recover from a hard limit, jog the axis back off it in the other direction (some systems need a limit override held while you do).

cards.q: Put these in order, from the middle of the travel outwards.
cards.why: Each layer catches what gets past the one before, with stopping room between them.

cards.title: Why limit switches are normally closed
cards.body:
Limit switches (and their inputs) are wired **normally closed**: the circuit is made while the axis is clear, and **breaks** when the limit is reached.

So a **broken wire**, a loose terminal or an unplugged switch also breaks the circuit, and the controller sees a limit and stops. The fault shows up as a stop, not as a limit that silently stops working.

The same idea makes stop buttons and many safety inputs normally closed.
cards.more:
With a normally open limit, the axis relies on a signal arriving to stop it. If the cable has been cut, the signal never comes, and the axis runs into its end stop.

With normally closed, the controller relies on a signal being present to keep moving. Cut the cable and the signal disappears, which is exactly what a limit looks like: the axis stops, and someone looks at the cable.

In the PLC or motion controller, the input is set as 'active low' for that reason: a 0 means 'at the limit'.

cards.q: A hard limit switch's cable is cut. With the switch wired normally closed, what happens?
options: The controller sees a limit and stops that way
Nothing until the axis reaches the switch
The axis runs on until the end stop
The controller loses its home position
cards.why: Normally closed means the circuit is made while clear; a cut cable breaks it just as reaching the limit would. The fault shows itself straight away instead of hiding.

cards.q: Put a switch-and-index homing sequence in order.
items: Search for the home switch at a fair speed
Stop, then back off until the switch clears
Creep back to the switch from the same side, and latch it
Carry on to the next index pulse and latch it
Apply the home offset and set the position
cards.why: Find it fast, measure it slowly, refine with the index, then set the coordinates.

cards.q: A motor with an encoder (one index pulse per motor turn) drives a {lead} mm lead screw through a {r}:1 gearbox. How far does the table move between index pulses?
cards.work: One motor turn is ${lead} \div {r} = {answer}$ mm of table travel
cards.why: The index comes once per motor turn. Through the gearbox, one motor turn is 1/{r} of a screw turn, so {lead} ÷ {r} mm. The home switch's edge should sit about half of this from an index pulse.
cards.hint: How far does one motor turn move the table?

cards.q: Why are software limits switched off (or ignored) until the axis has homed?
options: Until homed, the position they compare against is meaningless
Software limits slow down the homing search
Homing needs the axis to pass its limit switches
They are only for use in automatic mode
cards.why: A software limit is a position number. Before homing, the axis's position count starts wherever it powered up, so the limits would be in the wrong places. Once homed, they mean what they say.

cards.front: Why does a homing sequence always finish in the same direction?
cards.back: To take out backlash in the screw or gearbox (and the switch's hysteresis), so the same reading means the same place every time.

cards.front: When must a multi-turn absolute axis have its zero checked again?
cards.back: After anything that changes the link between encoder and machine: a crash, a slipped coupling, a motor or encoder change, or a lost battery on a battery-backed encoder.

cards.q: Can an axis's hard limit switches be relied on to protect someone working in the machine?
options: Not unless designed as a safety function
Yes: they stop the axis, so they are safe
Yes, if they are wired normally closed
Yes, if the software limits are also set
cards.why: Ordinary limits protect the machine. Protecting people needs a safety function designed and validated for it (EN ISO 13849: safety-rated switches and circuits, or a drive's safe limited position), plus guarding and safe working procedures.

cards.intro: A servo axis on a ball screw, run by a PLC. It has just been switched on, so its incremental encoder reads 0 wherever the carriage happens to be. Switch Enable on, then use the buttons.

ask.q: Home the axis, then move the carriage to 150 mm and leave it there.
fails: The drive is not enabled: switch Enable on first.
The PLC has stopped on a fault (see the Fault line). Clear the cause, press Reset, and try again.
It is not homed yet, so its position means nothing and the PLC refuses Move. Press Home and wait for the Homed lamp.
Homed, but not at 150 mm: set the Target to 150 mm and press Move.
Nearly: it is still moving. Let it settle, then check.
ask.hint: Watch the State line while it homes: search, back off, creep. Move only works once the Homed lamp is on.
ask.why: Until it homes, the axis only knows how far it has moved since power-up, so "150 mm" means nothing: the PLC refuses Move, and the software limits are not yet in force. Homing searches for the switch at 40 mm/s, backs off until it clears, then creeps back at 5 mm/s from the same side; where the switch makes is set to 0. After that the reading and the scale on the base agree, and Move goes to 150 mm.

cards.intro: The same axis has been reported as "won't home", or not quite right. Run it as you would on the machine: switch Enable on, press Home, try the jogs. Read the lamps, the State and Fault lines, and the LEDs on the PLC's inputs, against where the carriage really is.

ask.why: Where the sequence stops tells you most. Ran on to the − limit: the home switch was never seen. Backed off and never cleared: the switch is on all the time. Stopped on a + limit the moment it backed off: a limit says it is hit when it is not (normally closed, so a broken wire looks like a limit). Tripped on following error as soon as it was enabled: the drive's own feedback, not the switches.

cards.q: Which axis does not need to home after a power cut?
options: One with a multi-turn absolute encoder
One with an incremental encoder
A stepper with no encoder
One with a single-turn absolute encoder on a long screw
cards.why: A multi-turn absolute encoder reads its whole position at power-up. The others either count from power-up or only know the angle within one turn.

cards.q: Match each limit with what it is.
pairs: A position the controller will not command beyond
A switch that stops the axis if it overtravels
A buffer that physically stops it

cards.q: Why home to an index pulse after the switch?
options: It repeats to about one encoder count
It is faster than homing to a switch
It avoids the need for limit switches
It works without an encoder
cards.why: The index comes at the same angle every turn, so it is far more repeatable than a switch edge. The switch picks which turn.
